/itineraryStops/6/description.source_en:
**⟦G0⟧ (감천문화마을)** — nicknamed both **'Korea's Machu Picchu'** and **'Korea's Santorini'** — is a hillside neighborhood in Saha-gu, west Busan, whose pastel-painted houses cascade down in stepped rows over the slope. 

The settlement began in the **1920s-1930s** when the Busan administration relocated working-class residents away from the port. The village's character was set in **1955** when **~800 families (about 4,000 people) of the Taegeukdo religious community** — a uniquely Korean syncretic religion blending Buddhist, Confucian, and yin-yang elements, founded by **Jo Cheol-je** during the Japanese colonial period — settled here as Korean War refugees fleeing the North. 

The Taegeukdo philosophy of '**allowing others to prosper**' directly shaped the village's most distinctive feature: houses are intentionally tiered so that **no roof blocks the view of the house behind it**, with the entire community visible to the sky and the sea. Gamcheon remained one of Busan's poorest neighborhoods until **2009**, when the Korean Ministry of Culture launched the **'Dreaming of Machu Picchu in Busan'** public-art revitalization project, followed by the **'Miro Miro' (maze) project in 2010** — adding 22+ commissioned murals, sculptures, and art installations including the iconic **'Little Prince and Fox' bench** at the Sky Garden viewpoint. 

Gamcheon won the **2012 UN-HABITAT Asian Townscape Award** and now welcomes **~1.4 million visitors annually**. The visit follows the village's signature stamp-map walking route: from the entrance at the **Tourist Information Center**, up to **Sky Garden viewpoint** for the panoramic rainbow-roof shot, then down through the labyrinthine alleys past murals, hanbok rental shops, craft workshops, and small cafes. 

**The village is a living residential community** — quiet voices required, no drones, no flash photography into homes, and rubbish carried out. 

Hours **09:00-18:00 Mar-Oct / 09:00-17:00 Nov-Feb (info center)**; **village itself open 24h, FREE entry**.

/itineraryStops/7/whyOnRoute.source_en: **The quiet closer the buses skip.** After Gamcheon's crowds, Dakbatgol shows the same hillside Busan at living volume — murals, wish stairs, and a monorail that does the climbing. It closes the villages chapter ten minutes from the Nampo drop-off zone, so the day ends deep in local texture rather than in traffic.

/itineraryStops/7/description.source_en: **Dakbatgol (닥밭골)** is a hillside village in Busan's Seo-gu whose name remembers the **paper-mulberry (dak) fields** that once supplied Korea's traditional hanji paper-makers. Like Gamcheon it climbs a steep slope in tight lanes — but it never became a tour-bus stop, so its **mural alleys, hanji-motif artwork, and lookout points stay quiet and local**, laundry lines and all. The village's landmark is the **'wish stairs' (소망계단)** — a long, steep stair street painted with murals — and the **free incline monorail** that glides beside it, installed so the village's elderly residents could reach their homes; visitors ride it too, turning the steepest climb of the afternoon into a slow-motion viewpoint. It is the deliberately human-scale counterpoint to Gamcheon's fame, ten minutes before drop-off territory.

/itineraryStops/7/visitBasics/hours.source_en: Open village; monorail runs daytime hours (≈ 09:00–18:00, weather-dependent)

/itineraryStops/7/visitBasics/closed.source_en: Monorail may pause for maintenance or storm weather — the stairs remain open

/itineraryStops/7/visitBasics/walking.source_en: Steep lanes and stairs; the monorail covers the steepest section

/itineraryStops/8/whyOnRoute.source_en: Dakbatgol sits ten minutes from Nampo-dong, so the drop sequence starts almost immediately after the last stop — no dead transfer time. The west-to-east order covers KTX travelers (Busan Station), central hotels (Seomyeon), and beach hotels (Haeundae) without backtracking.

/itineraryStops/8/description.source_en: **Drop-offs run in sequence from the west side back east**: **Nampo-dong / Jagalchi area (~17:10)** — step off here for Busan's best evening food streets and the ⟦G0⟧ night scene; **Busan Station (~17:30)** for KTX connections; **Seomyeon (~17:50)** for the central hotel cluster; and **Haeundae (~18:20)** last. Choose your drop point with the guide during the afternoon — staying on to Haeundae is the longest ride but lands you by the beach for the evening.
